chapter: Opening and life on the road
title: The stickers on the baritone case and the reality of touring
summary: Smulyan explains that the stickers reflect airport-hotel-gig routines with little sightseeing, and that musicians are paid to travel.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe off-camera, for the Jazz Archive at Hamilton College, and I’m very happy to have Gary Smulyan here. And I want to start out asking about all those stickers on your baritone sax case.
What do you want to know?
Well, to people who aren’t that familiar with the life of a musician, it looks very exotic.
Yeah. I mean I think it looks like, oh, you’ve been to all these places, that must be the greatest thing.

Well you know the thing is, I think musicians hear that a lot. They’d say, oh, you’re a musician, you must lead a real amazing life, you get to go to all these places. But in many cases that’s not really the reality. The reality is you go to a lot of places but you see very little of those places because you go from the airport to the hotel to the sound check, to the concert, and back to the hotel and to the airport the next day. So unless, on rare occasions where we’re in a place for a week playing a club, or for a couple of days where we get a chance to actually take a walk and get out of the hotel and see something, a lot © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -1-

of times we’re just on the plane and, you know, switching, and you’re playing a lot of one-nighters and you’re just kind of hoofin’ it from place to place. So basically if I get a backstage pass or a sticker I just slap it on my case. So that’s — I mean I started doing that a long time ago and I just kind of continued.
But that is the reality of musicians on the road is that a lot of times you go to these amazingly cool places and it’s all New Jersey.
It’s all New Jersey. I like that. It reminds me of that often-quoted Phil Woods story about part of the jazz education should be getting on a bus and —

Yeah. Driving around the campus and that’s a lot of it. A lot of it is just — the traveling is — I mean I think we get paid to travel. You know the playing part is incidental. I mean you know sometimes we’ll travel for hours and hours to get to a place and then play for two hours, or not even two hours, sometimes we play a 75 minute set, and just get back on the plane and come home the next day.
